timeLimit: 1:00 per heat; three heats, best two count

competition.name: Competition #2: Asphalt Annihilation (Burnside Skatepark)
competition.rules: Three heats per skater; best two heats count; runs judged on style, difficulty and variety; points deducted for falling; bronze, silver and gold medals

goals.text: Competition #2 Asphalt Annihilation: three heats per skater, best two count, judged on style, difficulty and variety, points off for falling; bronze, silver, gold
Competition Park: a medal for a top-3 finish; the average of your top two runs is your final score

guidance: The giant eyeball is the level’s compass: you can see it across the park, and three gaps are named after it.
Every edge is painted yellow-black (VG): grindable coping and ledges read at a distance.
The bridge deck, pillars and girders are overhead from the first frame (LP1 0:19:49); the girder grind is in view the whole run, while its access (funbox + charged ollie) is not obvious.
Brand signage marks key objects: “flip” ads on the Triple Rail barriers, AXION banners on the pillars, the ZERO skull at the start (LP1).
Remake: dark, rainy lighting (LP12 0:27:10 loading card “It’s raining, it’s pouring …”) makes the lit bowls stand out.
Hidden on purpose: the top ledge tier is unpainted and broken, so it does not read as a grind line until you are up there.
designLogic: A real park, game-ified. The layout follows the famous DIY park (bowls, the hip Tony names as his favourite) and adds game objects: the eyeball paint, the twinkie bump and a girder line under the bridge.
Bowls dominate and transfers connect them. Tony’s favourite line is “transfers … in and out of the bowls”; almost every original gap is a transfer or an air over a bowl.
The hardest place is the real bridge structure overhead. Bridge Grind 800 and Bridge Gap 1000 make the architecture the challenge, the same idea as Chicago’s rafters.
Obstacles on a grind line: the struts force ollie-hops while grinding the girder. A rhythm test on a single beam.
Threading as a gap. Bridge Gap pays for passing through the struts without touching the girder. The remake turns that window into the logo’s hiding place.
Tiered ledges with deliberate breaks turn the biggest air into the longest descending grind, and a fall only drops you one tier.
One big launcher, many outcomes: the tall quarterpipe wall feeds Over Da Pool, the vert wall, the tiered ledges and the girder line (via the funbox).
A tiny object makes a big gap: the twinkie bump turns flat ground into a pool transfer (700).
Circuits pay for repetition. The U-quarterpipe/spine circuit awards three Transfer bonuses in one loop and is designed to be ridden counter-clockwise (G1 p112).
The start obstacle is part of a line. The Triple Rail finishes on the obstacle you started on, so the level loops back to its own spawn.
Remake: vertical tiers on one quarterpipe are scored separately (Bottom Shelf Lip 500 → Top Shelf Lip 1000). Height doubles the value.
Remake collectibles are paired high/low near the same supports: the plushie on a little white quarterpipe at a support’s foot, the logo inside the support above.
Failure is cheap everywhere: falls land in bowls or on the flat, never out of bounds, so a 1:00 heat can absorb a missed girder attempt.
remakeChanges: Setting: the remake’s Burnside is dark and rainy (LP12 0:27:05–0:29:20); the loading card reads “It’s raining, it’s pouring, but my skat[eboard] …”, and its PROTIP warns that the more times you use a trick in a run, the less it is worth (LP12 0:27:10; text partly cut off). That makes the variety judging explicit.
New gaps: Lippn’ The Bridge, Top Shelf Lip, Bottom Shelf Lip and Something in da Eye (lip tricks), Rollin’ The Hill (manual), Over da Pool Landing (a longer Over Da Pool).
Collectibles added: 2 stat points per style, the VV logo inside a bridge support and the alien plushie on a white quarterpipe by a support (PS12).
VG labels a “Wall Gap” that neither G1 nor PS12 lists.
LP12 shows the remake’s “Overtime!” finish during Burnside heats (0:28:15–0:28:25).
transfer: Through the struts: put the crystal inside the opening of a bridge support, between two struts. It is reachable by one aimed vert air from a nearby quarterpipe, or by a charged ollie (≈ 13.8 m reach at maximum charge) off a funbox. Make the window about 1.5–2 times the player’s jump width so it reads as a threading test.
Strut rhythm: a long girder grind with posts every few metres forces grind-ollie hops (≈ 2.4 m pop). Place the crystal on the girder after the last strut, so the reward follows the rhythm.

Tiered descent: three ledges stepping down from the top of a tall quarterpipe wall, with breaks shorter than a cruise ollie (≤ 9 m). Put the crystal at the top tier’s first break, so only players who land the huge air reach it; a fall drops them to a lower tier.
Landmark bowl as compass: give the level one unmistakable bowl (the eyeball) that is visible from everywhere, and orient all secrets relative to it in the level’s hints.
High/low pair: tease the crystal from a low, easy perch at the foot of the support (as the remake’s plushie does) and put the real crystal in the window above.
openQuestions: Spawn orientation: G1 calls the twinkie “to the right of where you start” and PS12 puts the eyeball pool to the right; VG places the twinkie far to the W of START. Which way does the spawn camera face after the intro pan?
Where exactly are the three ledge tiers (G1 p112) on the VG render, and are they the remake’s koi-fish quarterpipe ledges?
Girder height and strut spacing are not measurable from VG; no LP1 or TAS1 footage of the girder grind.
VG “Wall Gap” (S wall): points and requirement unknown; not in G1 or PS12.
The “quarterpipe by the semis” (G1 p114): the parked semis are not identifiable on the VG crop studied.
